title: Do we require and audit verification of AI-generated content before it is relied upon, submitted, or delivered externally?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether the organization has a mandatory, auditable verification step for AI-generated content used in professional or duty-of-care work, rather than trusting fluent AI output on the basis of its confident tone.

history.note: Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources).

question_text: Do we have a mandatory, auditable step requiring staff to verify AI-generated citations, facts, or recommendations against authoritative primary sources before that content is submitted to a court, delivered to a client, or otherwise relied upon — and how would we know if that step were being skipped, the way it apparently was in Mata v. Avianca and in the conduct underlying the FTC's DoNotPay settlement?
rationale: In Mata v. Avianca, a lawyer submitted a legal brief containing fabricated case citations generated by ChatGPT, resulting in court sanctions; in the DoNotPay matter, the FTC alleged the company's 'AI lawyer' service was never tested to confirm its output was comparable to advice from a human lawyer, resulting in a settlement.
follow_up_actions: Request the current AI output verification records for AI-assisted professional work product delivered in the last quarter.
Confirm verification is a mandatory, checked step rather than a policy statement with no enforcement mechanism.
Ask what proportion of AI-generated claims in reviewed work product required correction or were discarded, as a signal of underlying reliability.

citations.title: DoNotPay Settles FTC Allegations that it Deceived Consumers about the AI 'Lawyer' Service it Claims Can Substitute for Actual Legal Consultations
